content: Geranium maculatum, commonly known as the Spotted Geranium, Wood Geranium, or Wild Geranium, is a perennial herbaceous plant native to the woodlands of eastern North America. Its range extends from southern Manitoba and southwestern Quebec in Canada, down to Alabama in the United States, and westward to Oklahoma and South Dakota. This plant thrives in dry to moist wooded areas and is often found in abundance where it grows. The plant typically reaches a height of up to 60 cm and produces upright stems that are usually unbranched. It flowers during the spring to early summer months. The leaves are broad, measuring approximately 5 cm across, and are attached to petioles that can grow up to 30 cm long, emerging directly from the rootstock. These leaves are deeply divided into three or five segments, with each segment further cleft and toothed. The flowers of Geranium maculatum are 5–4 cm in diameter and feature five petals that are rose-purple, pale purple, or violet-purple in color, though white flowers are rare. Each flower has ten stamens and blooms in loose clusters of two to five at the tops of the stems. The flowering period typically occurs between April and June. The fruit of the plant is a capsule that opens when ripe, consisting of five cells, each containing a single seed. These seeds are attached to a long, beak-like column measuring 2–3 cm in length, which resembles a crane’s bill and arises from the center of the old flower. The rhizome of the plant is long and measures 5 to 10 cm in thickness, with numerous branches. It is covered with scars that indicate the remains of stems from previous years' growth. When dried, the rhizome exhibits a somewhat purplish internal coloration. After the seeds have ripened and dispersed, the plant enters dormancy in early summer. Geranium maculatum has been historically used in herbal medicine and is also cultivated as an ornamental garden plant.
